strengths: Addresses a clear clinical NLP resource gap with 8,767 synthetic examples covering 15 categories and providing spans, presence, temporality, and rationales. An openly available resource is practically valuable where access to clinical records is restricted.

Real-data experiments substantiate benefits for small-model classification. Prompt-tuned RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F on MIMIC-SBDH aligned, while standard RoBERTa improves from 72.38 to 80.71 on VA-SBDH. Multiple architectures, three independent runs, and training-size ablations strengthen this evidence.

Two experienced annotators review the entire 1,755-example synthetic test split, adjudicate disagreements, and correct annotations and rationales. The category-level error analysis provides useful transparency about the resource's limitations.

The manuscript documents generation prompts, all 45 seed examples, category mappings, and training configurations, and links a data/code/checkpoint release. The resource and supported classification improvements constitute a useful contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The broad improvement claims exceed the results. In Table 4, the strongest encoder NER baseline receives no macro-F improvement, and the dramatic T5 gain starts from an unusually unstable baseline (25.44 ± 18.24). Llama models show essentially no benefit in Table 14. The headline housing-insecurity improvement also rests on only 18 positive test examples; variation across training seeds does not capture uncertainty from this small test sample.

Evidence for reasoning distillation is limited to the synthetic test set. DSS improves macro-F by only 0.66 and 0.58 points for T5 and FLAN-T5, respectively, with the latter nonsignificant (p=0.36). Real clinical extraction could be evaluated without reference rationales, so their absence does not preclude testing transfer. These results support a modest auxiliary-supervision benefit but do not establish the claimed transfer of reasoning capability.

The annotation audit reveals substantial omissions and corrections: 286 updates, 142 discards, and 581 additions. Moreover, Appendix E.2 accepts any plausible category already selected by GPT-4 while requiring the more specific category when adding a missing annotation. This asymmetric policy can favor existing model annotations and limits the benchmark's consistency. The 71.06% Keep rate includes added annotations in its denominator; comparability with the reported human–human agreement requires clarification.

Important experimental controls and reporting details remain unclear. Appendix D.2 describes a matched-step comparison against MIMIC pretraining, but Table 13 does not separately identify those results and is also presented as the target-only baseline comparison. Oversampling or class-weighting controls would clarify the advantage over simpler imbalance interventions. The statistical testing procedure is insufficiently specified, particularly for the reported significance involving unstable T5 runs.

The distinctive coverage is only partly validated. Experiments retain positive, non-nested annotations and do not separately evaluate temporal or status prediction. Synthetic examples are also much shorter than the real examples (13.7 versus 35–47 words), with limited clinical shorthand and formatting diversity. Together with target-domain fine-tuning in every real-data experiment and restricted access to VA-SBDH, this narrows the demonstrated generalizability and independently reproducible evaluation scope.
